intro.title: Adding rows: INSERT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
So far every query only read data. This quest changes it. The database is a small lending library: `members` borrow `books`, each borrowing is a row in `loans`, some members owe `fines`, and new books wait in `arrivals`. Open **Tables** to see them. Today is 2026-10-24.

Nothing here can break: every **Run** and **Check** starts from a fresh copy of the database. A **Check** compares the tables afterwards with what was asked.

`INSERT INTO` adds a row. Name the columns, then give the values in the same order:

```
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined)
VALUES ('Hana Sato', 'hana.sato@example.com', '2026-10-24');
```

The result says **Done: 1 row changed.** To see the new row, add a query after it: `SELECT * FROM members;`. Statements run in order, so the query sees the change.

Columns you leave out get their **default**. In `members`, `status` defaults to `'active'`, and `id` is an `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`, which SQLite fills in by itself with the next free number. Columns with no default get `NULL`.

You can leave out the column list, but then you must give a value for every column, in the table's order. That breaks as soon as someone adds a column, so always name them.

Text goes in single quotes, as in `WHERE`. A single quote inside the text is written twice: `'The Baker''s Map'`. Missing values are written `NULL`, without quotes.

intro.title: Many rows at once
intro.bodyMarkdown:
One `INSERT` can add several rows: put a comma between the brackets of values.

```
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined) VALUES
  ('Hana Sato', 'hana.sato@example.com', '2026-10-24'),
  ('Ivo Petrov', NULL, '2026-10-24');
```

Rows often come from another table instead. `INSERT … SELECT` adds every row a query returns. The new books waiting in `arrivals` can go into `books` like this, with all their copies available:

```
INSERT INTO books (title, author, copies, available)
SELECT title, author, copies, copies
FROM arrivals;
```

The query's columns are matched to the listed columns by position, so `copies` is used twice: once for `copies`, once for `available`. Everything you know about queries works here: `WHERE`, joins, `GROUP BY`, `COALESCE` and fixed values like `'2026-10-24'`.

Write and run the `SELECT` on its own first. When it shows exactly the rows you want to add, put the `INSERT INTO … (…)` line above it.

FROM arrivals;

challenges.title: Medium: Overdue fines
challenges.promptMarkdown: Give every member with an overdue loan (not returned, due before `2026-10-24`) a fine of `1.0`, one row per member. None of them has a fine yet.

INSERT INTO fines (member_id, amount)
SELECT DISTINCT member_id, 1.0
FROM loans
WHERE returned IS NULL AND due < '2026-10-24';

intro.title: Changing rows: UPDATE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`UPDATE` changes values in rows that are already there. `SET` says what changes, and `WHERE` says which rows:

```
UPDATE loans
SET returned = '2026-10-24'
WHERE id = 6;
```

**Without `WHERE`, every row changes.** `UPDATE loans SET returned = '2026-10-24';` marks every loan in the library as returned today. In a real database there is no undo, so the habit that matters most here is this: write the `WHERE` first, try it in a `SELECT`, and only then turn it into an `UPDATE`.

```
SELECT * FROM members WHERE joined < '2022-01-01';
-- happy with those rows? then:
UPDATE members SET status = 'inactive' WHERE joined < '2022-01-01';
```

The result tells you how many rows changed, which is a quick check that the `WHERE` matched what you expected. Several columns change at once with commas: `SET copies = 3, available = 3`.

Watch out for `NULL` in `WHERE`, as always. `WHERE status <> 'suspended'` skips Esther, whose status is missing, because comparing with `NULL` isn't true. Add `OR status IS NULL`, or use SQLite's `IS NOT`, which treats `NULL` like a value: `WHERE status IS NOT 'suspended'`.

intro.title: Calculated updates
intro.bodyMarkdown:
The new value in `SET` can be calculated, usually from the row's own values. Every book gets one more copy:

```
UPDATE books
SET copies = copies + 1,
    available = available + 1;
```

On the right of `=`, a column means the row's value **before** the update. So `copies + 1` reads the old count and stores one more, and all the assignments in one `SET` see the same old values. That makes swapping two columns easy: `SET copies = available, available = copies`.

Any expression works: functions, text joined with `||`, dates, and `CASE` to choose a different value for different rows:

```
UPDATE members
SET status = CASE
  WHEN joined < '2024-01-01' THEN 'long-time'
  ELSE 'new'
END
WHERE status IS NOT 'suspended';
```

Running a calculated update twice usually does it twice: two runs of `copies + 1` add two copies. In this app every Run starts from fresh data, but in a real database you'd check the numbers before running it again.

intro.title: Updates that use other tables
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Often the rows to change are picked by looking at another table. Subqueries work in an UPDATE's `WHERE` just as in a `SELECT`. Suspend every member who has an overdue loan:

```
UPDATE members
SET status = 'suspended'
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT member_id FROM loans
  WHERE returned IS NULL AND due < '2026-10-24'
);
```

A correlated subquery in `SET` works out a different value for each row. Some `available` numbers in `books` are wrong, so recount them from the loans that are still out:

```
UPDATE books
SET available = copies - (
  SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans
  WHERE loans.book_id = books.id AND loans.returned IS NULL
);
```

Inside the subquery, `books.id` is the row being updated. Leaving out that link is a classic mistake: the subquery then counts every open loan in the library and gives every book the same wrong number.

SQLite also has `UPDATE … FROM`, which joins another table in, so its columns can be used in `SET` and `WHERE`. Add the arriving copies to books that are already on the shelf:

```
UPDATE books
SET copies = books.copies + a.copies,
    available = books.available + a.copies
FROM arrivals AS a
WHERE a.title = books.title;
```

intro.title: Removing rows: DELETE
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`DELETE FROM` removes the rows that match its `WHERE`:

```
DELETE FROM loans
WHERE id = 10;
```

As with `UPDATE`, **without `WHERE` every row goes**: `DELETE FROM loans;` empties the table (the table itself stays, with no rows). Use the same habit: write the `WHERE` as a `SELECT` first, look at the rows, then change `SELECT *` to `DELETE`.

```
SELECT * FROM loans WHERE returned < '2026-09-01';
-- those are the ones? then:
DELETE FROM loans WHERE returned < '2026-09-01';
```

Subqueries pick rows by looking at other tables. Remove the fines of people who are no longer members (the fine for member 9 belongs to nobody):

```
DELETE FROM fines
WHERE member_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM members);
```

Deleting a row doesn't touch other tables. If you delete a member, their loans still point to an id that no longer exists. The quest on designing tables shows how foreign keys can stop that; for now, it is up to you to delete or change the related rows too.

intro.title: Insert or update: ON CONFLICT
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Some columns can't hold the same value twice. In `fines`, `member_id` is the primary key, so each member has at most one row, and in `members` each `email` is `UNIQUE`. Inserting a second fine for member 2 fails with **UNIQUE constraint failed: fines.member_id**.

Often you want "add it, or if it is already there, change it". That is called an **upsert**:

```
INSERT INTO fines (member_id, amount)
VALUES (2, 1.5)
ON CONFLICT (member_id) DO UPDATE
SET amount = amount + excluded.amount;
```

`ON CONFLICT (member_id)` names the column whose clash you are handling. If there is no clash, the row is inserted. If there is, `DO UPDATE` changes the existing row instead. `excluded` means the row you tried to insert, so `excluded.amount` is 1.5 here, and `amount` alone is the existing row's value.

`ON CONFLICT … DO NOTHING` simply skips rows that clash. `INSERT OR IGNORE` is a shorter way to say the same thing.

`INSERT OR REPLACE` looks similar but works differently: it **deletes** the clashing row and inserts the new one. Any column you didn't give is lost and goes back to its default. Use `DO UPDATE` when you only want to change some columns.

One detail: when the rows come from `INSERT … SELECT`, SQLite can mistake `ON CONFLICT` for the `ON` of a join. If the SELECT has no `WHERE`, add `WHERE true` before `ON CONFLICT` to avoid that.

intro.title: Seeing what changed: RETURNING
intro.bodyMarkdown:
`INSERT`, `UPDATE` and `DELETE` normally only say how many rows they changed. Add `RETURNING` at the end and they also show the rows themselves, like a `SELECT`:

```
INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined)
VALUES ('Hana Sato', 'hana.sato@example.com', '2026-10-24')
RETURNING id, name;
```

That is the easiest way to find out the id SQLite gave a new row. After an `UPDATE`, `RETURNING` shows the new values; after a `DELETE`, it shows the rows that were removed, which makes a handy record of what went:

```
DELETE FROM loans
WHERE returned < '2026-09-01'
RETURNING id, member_id, returned;
```

After `RETURNING` you can list columns, use `*`, calculate and rename with `AS`, just like in a `SELECT` list. You can't use aggregates like `COUNT` there, and the rows come back in no particular order.

`RETURNING` arrived in SQLite 3.35 (2021). PostgreSQL has it too; other databases have their own ways of doing the same thing.

intro.title: Easy side quest: Front desk day
intro.bodyMarkdown:
You're on the library's front desk today, 2026-10-24. People come in to join, borrow, return, renew and pay. Each challenge is one visitor; get the data right for each.

Anything that changes two tables goes in a transaction. A book that goes out lowers `available`; a book that comes back raises it.
intro.sandboxCode: SELECT * FROM loans WHERE returned IS NULL;

challenges.title: Easy: Joining
challenges.promptMarkdown: `Hana Sato` (`hana.sato@example.com`) joins today. Add her and return her `id` so you can write it on her card.
challenges.hint: `INSERT INTO members (name, email, joined) VALUES (…) RETURNING id;`

tests.label: The members table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Easy: Borrowing
challenges.promptMarkdown: Member 2 borrows book 7, due back on `2026-11-07`. In one transaction, add the loan and lower book 7's `available`.
challenges.hint: BEGIN; INSERT INTO loans …; UPDATE books …; COMMIT;

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Medium: Returning
challenges.promptMarkdown: Loan 3 comes back. In one transaction, raise the `available` of its book (found from the loan) and mark the loan returned today.
challenges.hint: Update books `WHERE id = (SELECT book_id FROM loans WHERE id = 3)` first, then the loan.

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Medium: Renewing
challenges.promptMarkdown: The borrower of loan 8 renews it: if it is still out, its new due date is 14 days from today.
challenges.hint: `date('2026-10-24', '+14 days')` gives the new due date. Only change the loan if `returned IS NULL`.

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Hard: Paying up
challenges.promptMarkdown: Member 6 pays `3.0`. In one transaction, take it off their fine and delete their fine row if nothing is left to pay.
challenges.hint: UPDATE fines … WHERE member_id = 6; DELETE FROM fines WHERE member_id = 6 AND amount <= 0;

tests.label: The fines table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM fines ORDER BY member_id

challenges.title: Hard: Reminders
challenges.promptMarkdown: At closing time, set the status of every member with an overdue loan (still out, due before today) to `reminded`, and return their `id` and `name` for the reminder letters.
challenges.hint: `UPDATE members SET status = 'reminded' WHERE id IN (…overdue member ids…) RETURNING id, name;`
challenges.solution:
UPDATE members
SET status = 'reminded'
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT member_id FROM loans
  WHERE returned IS NULL AND due < '2026-10-24'
)
RETURNING id, name;

tests.label: The members table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id

intro.title: Medium side quest: Stock take
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Once a year the library counts its books. Some numbers in `books` are wrong, new copies have arrived, one book was lost and some books nobody borrows any more.

A book's `available` should always be its `copies` minus its loans still out.

challenges.title: Easy: Recount
challenges.promptMarkdown: Set every book's `available` to its copies minus its loans still out.
challenges.hint: `SET available = copies - (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM loans WHERE loans.book_id = books.id AND loans.returned IS NULL)`.

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Medium: The wrong way round
challenges.promptMarkdown: A book with more copies available than it owns must have its two numbers swapped. Swap `copies` and `available` for every such book.
challenges.hint: `SET copies = available, available = copies WHERE available > copies`.

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Medium: Unpack the arrivals
challenges.promptMarkdown: In one transaction: add the arriving copies to books already on the shelf (same title), insert the other arrivals as new books (1 copy when the number is missing, all available), then empty `arrivals`.
challenges.hint: UPDATE books … FROM arrivals …; INSERT INTO books … SELECT … WHERE title NOT IN (SELECT title FROM books); DELETE FROM arrivals;

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

tests.label: The arrivals table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM arrivals ORDER BY title, author, copies

challenges.title: Medium: Lost
challenges.promptMarkdown: Member 1 lost book 5 (loan 4). In one transaction: mark loan 4 returned today, take one copy off book 5 (its `available` stays as it is), and add a `10.0` replacement charge to member 1's fine, creating the row if needed.
challenges.hint: UPDATE loans …; UPDATE books SET copies = copies - 1 WHERE id = 5; an upsert into fines.

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

tests.label: The fines table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM fines ORDER BY member_id

challenges.title: Hard: Gathering dust
challenges.promptMarkdown: Withdraw the books that have no loan borrowed on or after `2026-09-01` and none still out. In one transaction, delete their loans, then the books.
challenges.hint: Pick them with `NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM loans WHERE loans.book_id = books.id AND (borrowed >= '2026-09-01' OR returned IS NULL))`. Delete the loans whose book_id is one of those books first; then the books with no loans left can go.

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Hard: More copies of the popular ones
challenges.promptMarkdown: In one transaction: recount `available` for every book, then give each book with no copies available one more copy (raise `copies` and `available` by 1), returning the `id`, `title`, `copies` and `available` of those books. Then commit.
challenges.hint: The recount UPDATE, then `UPDATE books SET copies = copies + 1, available = available + 1 WHERE available = 0 RETURNING id, title, copies, available;`, then COMMIT.

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

questions.prompt: What should `available` always be?

choices.label: copies minus the loans still out

questions.explanation: Every copy is either on the shelf or out on loan.

questions.prompt: Does `SET copies = available, available = copies` really swap them?

choices.label: No, both end up the same
Yes: both assignments use the old values

questions.explanation: SET reads all the old values before changing anything.

questions.prompt: When unpacking arrivals, why update the existing books before inserting the new ones?

choices.label: Otherwise the new rows would also match the title and get the copies twice

questions.explanation: After the INSERT, every arrival's title would be in books.

questions.prompt: Why does a lost book lower `copies` but not `available`?

choices.label: The lost copy was out on loan, so it was never counted as available

questions.explanation: The shelf has the same number of copies as before.

questions.prompt: Which keyword, at the end of an UPDATE, shows the changed rows?
questions.explanation: `… RETURNING id, title;`

questions.prompt: Why delete the loans before the books when withdrawing books?

choices.label: So no loans are left pointing to missing books

questions.explanation: Children first, then the rows they point to.

intro.title: Hard side quest: Data clean-up
intro.bodyMarkdown:
Years of quick fixes have left the library's data messy: capital letters in emails, missing statuses, a member entered twice, a loan typed in twice, fines for nobody, and counts that don't add up.

Fix each problem with as few statements as you can, and use a transaction when a fix touches more than one table.

challenges.title: Medium: Lower-case emails
challenges.promptMarkdown: Change every email to lower case, updating only the rows that change.
challenges.hint: `SET email = LOWER(email) WHERE email <> LOWER(email)`.

tests.label: The members table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Medium: Missing statuses
challenges.promptMarkdown: Set the status of every member whose status is missing to `active`.
challenges.hint: `WHERE status IS NULL`.

tests.label: The members table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Hard: One person, one record
challenges.promptMarkdown: Members with the same name are the same person. In one transaction, move all loans to the lowest id for that name, then delete the other members with that name.
challenges.hint: The same two statements as "Merge every duplicate" in the last stage.

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

tests.label: The members table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM members ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Hard: Typed twice
challenges.promptMarkdown: Delete the duplicate loans (same member, book and borrowed date), keeping the lowest id of each.
challenges.hint: `WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM loans GROUP BY member_id, book_id, borrowed)`.

tests.label: The loans table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM loans ORDER BY id

challenges.title: Hard: Fines that make sense
challenges.promptMarkdown: Delete the fines that belong to no member, and the fines of 0 or less, in one statement.
challenges.hint: `WHERE member_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM members) OR amount <= 0`.
challenges.solution:
DELETE FROM fines
WHERE member_id NOT IN (SELECT id FROM members) OR amount <= 0;

tests.label: The fines table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM fines ORDER BY member_id

challenges.title: Hard: Counts that add up
challenges.promptMarkdown: In one transaction, first swap `copies` and `available` for the books where available is bigger than copies (they were typed the wrong way round), then recount `available` for every book from the loans still out.
challenges.hint: The swap UPDATE with `WHERE available > copies`, then the recount UPDATE. The order matters.

tests.label: The books table is right afterwards
tests.assertion: SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY id

questions.prompt: Why `WHERE email <> LOWER(email)` when lowering emails?

choices.label: So only the rows that actually change are updated

questions.explanation: The rows-changed count then shows how many were fixed.

questions.prompt: Which finds missing statuses?
questions.explanation: = NULL is never true.

questions.prompt: When merging duplicates, why move the loans before deleting the members?

choices.label: The UPDATE looks up each member's name, which needs the duplicate rows to still exist

questions.explanation: After the DELETE, the duplicate ids would have no name to look up.

questions.prompt: Which keeps the first of each group of duplicate loans?

choices.label: `DELETE … WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) … GROUP BY …)`

questions.explanation: Delete every id that is not the smallest of its group.

questions.prompt: Which keyword joins two conditions so a row matching either one is deleted?
questions.explanation: `WHERE … OR …`.

questions.prompt: Why swap before recounting in "Counts that add up"?

choices.label: The recount uses copies, which is wrong until the swap fixes it

questions.explanation: Recounting first would subtract from the wrong number.
